title: What questions should you ask at the end of a consulting interview?
description: Good and bad questions to ask your interviewer at the end of a consulting interview, with examples that show curiosity and research.
hook: "Do you have any questions for me?" is not a formality. It is your last chance to show curiosity and leave a good impression, and it is a genuine chance to learn about the firm.
body:
The question

Do you have any questions for me?

A weak answer

What is the culture like?" or "How many hours do you work?

Why it falls short: Generic and easy to answer from a website, or framed in a way that may sound like you are mainly worried about workload.

A strong answer

You mentioned you moved from the healthcare practice into private equity work. What made you switch, and how did the firm help you make that move?" or "What's something you've learned on your current project that surprised you?

Why it works: Personal, specific to the interviewer, and invites a real conversation. It shows you were listening and are curious about the work.

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "Do you have any questions for me?" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.

Ask for insight you cannot get from the firm's website

The final minutes of an interview are a chance to learn about the role and show how you think. Generic questions such as "What is the culture like?" are hard to answer meaningfully. Better questions invite the interviewer to describe a real decision, trade-off or experience.

For someone interviewing for generalist consulting, you might ask: "On the last project you enjoyed, what made the team effective when the problem was still unclear?" For a candidate drawn to implementation: "How does your team know a recommendation has actually changed a client's behaviour six months later?" For an experienced hire: "Which skills do people joining from industry tend to underestimate in their first year?" These are examples, not a script to fire through mechanically.

Match the question to the person. A consultant can explain their daily work, feedback and team dynamics. A partner can discuss how client needs are changing and how the office builds new capabilities. A recruiter is usually best placed to clarify logistics, training and process. Respect what the person is able to know.

Listen to the response and ask one follow-up if it is genuinely interesting. A two-minute conversation about a real project is more memorable than reading five polished questions from a list. Avoid questions whose answers are already on the careers page unless you are asking about how the advertised policy works in practice.
